result:
I want to write about something small and almost invisible: the way ordinary moments gather weight after we’ve lived them.

There are minutes you don’t notice while they’re happening. A cup of tea cooling on a desk. Light moving across a wall in the late afternoon. Someone laughing in another room. The sound of a train passing far away, carrying strangers toward lives as complicated as your own. At the time, none of it feels important. It is just weather, just noise, just the background hum of being alive.

But later, some of those moments return. They rise up when you least expect them, wearing a different kind of light. Suddenly the cup of tea is not just a cup of tea, but peace, or solitude, or a version of yourself you didn’t know you were about to lose. The laugh in the other room becomes unbearable in its sweetness. The train becomes distance, longing, departure, possibility.

I think this is why people keep photographs, journals, and songs. Not because we want to preserve the exact facts of our lives, but because we know instincts will betray us. We know we will forget the texture of certain days. We know we will misremember ourselves. We collect fragments because the whole story is too fluid, too quick, too generous with its disappearing acts.

And yet, maybe forgetting is part of the beauty. A moment that can be forgotten can also be rediscovered. A memory that changes over time means we are not fixed creatures. We keep rewriting ourselves without realizing it. The person you were five years ago would not necessarily recognize the person you are now—not because your face has changed, but because your attention has changed. What you love has changed. What you fear has shifted. The questions you once asked have gone quiet while new ones have taken their place.

I like the idea that identity is less like a statue and more like a river. It has a shape, a direction, a name—but it is never the same twice. You can stand at its edge and think you understand it, but it has already moved on.

So if I were to dedicate my life to any single practice, I think it would be attention. Not perfect attention, not constant mindfulness, not the kind that becomes performance or obligation. Just gentle, stubborn attention. The kind that notices. The kind that says: this too existed, and I was here for it.

Because maybe that’s enough.
